title: An evaluation of online information acquisition in US news deserts
screen_reason: Behavioural browsing-log study (Microsoft Edge desktop telemetry, ~10% of US desktop browsing, Aug-Sep 2021) that reports county-level views of low-quality news domains normalised by total browser requests (per one million requests). These are shares of what people actually consumed that came from a domain-list of unreliable sources, i.e. EXPOSURE estimates with an explicit denominator (total requests). The paper's aim is a news-desert comparison, but descriptive medians are reported for each county stratum, so it is included under the 'aim is something else but a descriptive share is reported' rule.

estimates.platform: Microsoft Edge desktop browser telemetry (all web browsing)
estimates.measure_type: % of total desktop browser requests that were views of low-quality news domains, median county with no local newspaper (news desert)
estimates.value_raw: median=721 low-quality views per one million requests (news deserts)
estimates.denominator: one million total Microsoft Edge browser requests in the county (all web activity, not only news), median across US counties with no local newspaper
estimates.definition: a view (request) of a domain appearing on at least two of four low-quality-domain lists (three academic lists plus Media Bias/Fact Check), >1300 domains in total
estimates.misinfo_def: "We use the term low-quality to encompass sites that have been rated as poor information sources by academic or fact-checking groups."
estimates.n: 1,000,000 browser requests (normalising denominator) per county; telemetry covers roughly 10% of US desktop browsing activity, millions of users; exact county count not stated
estimates.source_quote: In fact, news deserts appear to view less low-quality information per million requests (median=721) than locations with two or more local papers (median=1461).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Domain-level lists: a site counts as low-quality if identified by at least two of four sources - three academic domain lists (Chen et al. 2021; Hounsel et al. 2020; Pennycook & Rand 2019) and the fact-checking group Media Bias/Fact Check; final list >1300 domains. No inter-rater reliability statistic reported (intersection rule used instead).
estimates.moderator_quote: For each county, we also collect the total amount of daily browser traffic. This number is used to re-scale our measures so that locations are more directly comparable. Each content type is normalized by the total requests for the county and then multiplied by one million.
estimates.notes: Value converted from the verbatim rate 721 per 1,000,000 requests to 0.0721% (same denominator, exact unit change; no cross-category sum or complement). This is a MEDIAN across counties in the news-desert stratum, not a pooled share of all requests - the paper reports no national pooled figure. Denominator is ALL browser requests (whole web diet), not news requests, so the share is very small by construction and is not comparable to news-diet-based estimates. Data-collection window as printed ends 'September 31, 2021' (a date that does not exist).

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted: (1) all OLS regression coefficients for news-desert status on views of low-quality news, national news and pink slime, and on social-media/search-engine referrals to low-quality sites (M1-M3, e.g. beta=-18.22, SE=47.50) - these are effect sizes, not shares with a denominator; (2) Figure 1's daily average visits per million requests for national news, low-quality news and pink slime - the values are only plotted, no numbers are given in the text, and the pink slime series is described qualitatively as 'almost no traffic'; (3) 'views for national news are over an order of magnitude larger than low-quality news' - a ratio, not a share; (4) the referral outcome (views of low-quality sites referred by social media or search engines per million referrals) - the paper reports only regression coefficients, never a level, so no share is available; (5) 'more than 25% of U.S. newspapers ceased operations' and similar background figures - not misinformation prevalence, and cited from elsewhere. UNCERTAIN: whether a 'per million total requests' rate should count as a prevalence share at all. The denominator is the entire desktop browsing diet (all web activity, not just news), which makes the value roughly two orders of magnitude smaller than news-diet-based exposure estimates; if the review restricts EXPOSURE to news-diet denominators, these rows should be dropped rather than pooled.

rob.design: County-level observational analysis of opt-in Microsoft Edge desktop telemetry (anonymised and aggregated at collection; roughly 10% of US desktop browsing activity, millions of users), 1 August - 'September 31' 2021; unit of analysis county-day and county. No response rate (telemetry, opt-in diagnostic sharing; authors note desktop browsing skews older and is not representative of all Americans). Misinformation coding is domain-level, not human coding of items: a site is low-quality if it appears on at least 2 of 4 published lists (3 academic, 1 fact-checking organisation), >1300 domains; no kappa or inter-rater reliability reported, the 2-of-4 intersection rule serving as the robustness device. Analysis by OLS with coarsened exact matching (M2) and state and day fixed effects (M3), SEs clustered on state-month. Data available from corresponding author on request only.
rob.item6_quote: We use the term low-quality to encompass sites that have been rated as poor information sources by academic or fact-checking groups. We construct our list of low-quality information sources by consulting a variety of existing work on the subject. In total, we use four sources that maintain lists of low-quality sites: three lists of domains complied by academic researchers53–55; and one from a fact-checking and media accountability groups (Media Bias/Fact Check). For our analysis, we consider a site to be low-quality if it has been identified by at least two of the sources.
rob.item10_quote: In fact, news deserts appear to view less low-quality information per million requests (median=721) than locations with two or more local papers (median=1461).
